items.prompt: Ana says "grab the keys" meaning the house keys. Ben brings the car keys. What went wrong?
choices: One word named two different things
Ben ignored a clear instruction
Ana picked a badly chosen word
The two sets looked too alike
items.explanation: Both were using the word sensibly; they just meant different things by it.

items.prompt: Billing counts 1,200 customers and Support counts 4,800. Who is wrong?
choices: Support, because its number is larger
Billing, because the smaller number cannot be complete
Both, because the totals must match
Neither, because they count different things
items.explanation: Billing counts paying accounts and Support counts ticket submitters, so the numbers answer different questions.

items.prompt: In Billing's meaning, what is a Customer?
choices: Any person who opens a support ticket
A visitor who browses the website
The paying account, one per company
Anyone who ever signed a contract
items.explanation: Billing tracks who owns and pays the invoices.

items.prompt: In Support's meaning, what is a Customer?
choices: The company that pays the invoice
Whoever opened the support ticket
The manager who approves payments
A user who only created an account
items.explanation: Support tracks the people asking for help, often several per company.

items.prompt: Why did the single customers table cause trouble?
choices: It silently encoded one team's meaning
It was built with too many columns for one query
It was missing a primary key
It lived on the wrong server
items.explanation: Every other team's code inherited the first team's meaning without anyone noticing.

items.prompt: An executive gets two different customer counts. What is the best fix?
choices: Delete one team's report
Average the two numbers
Ask the executive to stop asking
State which concept each number counts
items.explanation: Naming what is being counted makes both numbers correct and usable.

items.prompt: Using this unit's made-up data, how many ticket submitters per paying account on average?
choices: 6 contacts per account
3 contacts per account
4 contacts per account
0.25 contacts per account
items.explanation: 4,800 divided by 1,200 is 4.

items.prompt: When does a shared word become a problem?
choices: Whenever two teams share any word
When teams quietly mean different things
Only when the word is long
Only when the word appears in the code or a database table
items.explanation: Sharing a word is harmless; hidden disagreement about its meaning is the risk.

items.prompt: Team A calls a person a "client" and team B calls the same kind of person a "customer", with identical rules for both. Is this the same problem as Billing and Support?
choices: Yes, because the two words are spelled differently
No, it is one concept with two labels
Yes, because two teams are involved
No, because neither word is correct
items.explanation: The collision in this unit is one word covering two concepts with different rules. Two labels for one concept is a naming inconsistency, not a hidden second concept.
items.reference:
One word, two concepts
💳 Billing: Customer = the paying account (1,200 in this unit's made-up data)
🎫 Support: Customer = whoever opened a ticket (4,800)
🗃️ One table called customers hides the difference
Why: a shared word is not a shared meaning; each team can be right about its own number and still disagree with the other.
items.learnMore:
Same label, different concept

When two groups use one word for different things, neither is wrong. The cost shows up later, in reports and code that quietly assume one meaning.

Common mistake

Deciding which team is right instead of asking what each one counts.
items.reflection: Think of a word that two groups around you use differently, such as a deadline or a done. What does each group mean, and when did the difference last cost something?

items.prompt: What is ubiquitous language?
choices: Business words and code words kept identical and precise
One programming language used by every team
A glossary printed only for new hires
A style guide for variable name casing
items.explanation: It is about shared meaning between the business and the code.

items.prompt: Who is a domain expert?
choices: The engineer who wrote the module for that part
The longest-serving person on the team
Whoever manages the database server
Someone who knows that part of the business

items.prompt: Experts say "grace period". What should the code call it?
choices: A private abbreviation only engineers know
A generic name such as state2
A name that means grace period
A numeric code from a lookup sheet
items.explanation: The code name should be recognizable to the expert who coined the term.

items.prompt: What does drift mean here?
choices: Servers slowly slow down as the data keeps growing over time
Code words slowly stop matching business words
Teams slowly stop attending meetings
Data slowly grows past its limit
items.explanation: Drift is the gap that opens when nobody keeps the vocabulary aligned.

items.prompt: What is a good sign that the language is working?
choices: Experts can read model names and recognize them
The code has very few comments
The glossary is long and detailed
Every class has a short name
items.explanation: Recognition by the people who know the business is the test.

items.prompt: Who should help decide what a business word means?
choices: Engineers alone, decided once at project start
Whoever wrote the first database table
The team with the most staff
The people who do that work, with engineers
items.explanation: Meaning comes from the business, so its practitioners must be in the conversation.

items.prompt: Two people in a meeting seem to use one word differently. What is the best first move?
choices: Vote on a single winning definition right there and then
Skip the word and move on
Ask each to say exactly what they count
Let the louder person decide
items.explanation: Surfacing the actual definitions comes before any fix.

items.prompt: What does a new engineer gain from a precise shared language?
choices: They no longer need to ask anyone anything again
They can read the code and learn the business
They can skip learning the domain
They can rename things freely
items.explanation: Names that carry business meaning teach the domain as they are read.

items.prompt: The code stores a subscription state as the letters A, B and C. Experts say active, grace period and cancelled. What is the best change?
choices: Add a comment table mapping letters to terms
Rename the states to the experts' terms, agreed with them
Keep the letters but document them in a wiki
Let each engineer pick their own readable names
items.explanation: The point is that the code itself speaks the business language. A side document leaves the translation in people's heads.
items.reference:
Words that match
🗣️ Experts say: grace period
💻 Code says: GracePeriod, not state2
🔁 Same word in meetings, tickets and code
Why: when speech and code use the same precise words, nobody has to translate, and mistakes in translation cannot happen.

Treating a glossary on a wiki as the practice itself, when the code and meetings still use other words.

items.prompt: What is a bounded context?
choices: A boundary where a term has one precise meaning
A firewall between two servers
A limit on how many teams exist
A rule about maximum code size
items.explanation: It scopes a meaning, it is not a technical barrier.

items.prompt: Inside Billing's context, what does Customer mean?
choices: The person who opened a ticket
A user browsing the site
A prospect on a mailing list
The paying account
items.explanation: Billing's context is built around invoices and who owns them.

items.prompt: Inside Support's context, what does Customer mean?
choices: The company that pays invoices
The person who signed the contract
The ticket submitter
The manager who approves spending
items.explanation: Support's context is built around people asking for help.

items.prompt: Is it a bug that a word differs between contexts?
choices: Yes, every word needs one meaning
No, scoped meanings are expected
Yes, unless the teams are small
No, but only in older systems
items.explanation: Different meanings outside the boundary are the reason the boundary exists.

items.prompt: What must exist at the boundary between two contexts?
choices: An explicit relationship between the concepts
A shared database table
A single merged definition
A weekly status meeting
items.explanation: Without the link, the contexts just disagree silently.

items.prompt: How many billing accounts does each support contact belong to here?
choices: Exactly two
As many as they like
None until they pay
Exactly one
items.explanation: A company's employees all link to their employer's billing account.

items.prompt: Why not simply force Billing's definition on everyone?
choices: It makes the code run slower under heavy load
It breaks the invoice format
It deletes information Support needs
It needs more servers
items.explanation: Support must count individual submitters, and one-per-account hides them.

items.prompt: Bounded contexts usually follow what?
choices: Which programming language each team happens to use
How the business itself is organized
How large each table is
The order the teams were hired
items.explanation: A team, subsystem or process often marks where a meaning is stable.

items.prompt: A dashboard shows "4,800 support contacts across 1,200 billing accounts". What makes this statement possible?
choices: Both teams adopting a single merged Customer table
The explicit link from contacts to accounts
Both teams using Billing's definition
Rounding the two counts together
items.explanation: The boundary relationship says which contact belongs to which account, so the two labelled counts can sit side by side.
items.reference:
Two scoped meanings, one link
💳 Billing context: Customer = BillingAccount
🎫 Support context: Customer = SupportContact
🔗 Each SupportContact belongs to exactly one BillingAccount
Why: scoping each meaning and naming the link keeps both numbers correct and lets one report combine them.
items.learnMore:
A boundary around where a meaning holds

A bounded context is drawn where the business itself divides: a team, a subsystem or a process. Inside it a term has one meaning. At its edge, an explicit relationship says how it connects to the next context.

Common mistake

Splitting the names but never defining the relationship between them.
items.reflection: Think of a boundary in daily life where a word changes meaning, such as between two workplaces or two sports. How do people at the edge translate?

items.prompt: What does modeling a rule mean?
choices: The code enforces what the business allows
The code stores every value as text
The code logs every change made
The code is split into smaller files
items.explanation: A modeled rule refuses changes the business would not accept.

items.prompt: What order can SubscriptionStatus move through in this unit?
choices: Cancelled, then active, then grace period
Grace period, then cancelled, then active
Any order, as long as it ends somewhere
Active, then grace period, then cancelled
items.explanation: The grace period sits between active and cancelled.

choices: Yes, whenever a user asks through the account page
Yes, if an admin clicks twice
No, not without the grace period
No, but only on weekends
items.explanation: That is the rule the model encodes.

items.prompt: A status column accepts any string. What does it store?
choices: The business rules, fully enforced
Data, without the rules about it
Only the legal values
A history of all previous values
items.explanation: Nothing in a bare column says which values may follow which.

Never below 10% under any case
Always exactly 25% for new users

Domain experts
items.explanation: They are the people who would say the rule out loud.

items.prompt: Where should a rule live so that every caller gets it?
choices: Only in the user interface
Only in a wiki page
In the domain model itself
Only in a code comment
items.explanation: Anything that reaches the model then passes through the rule.

items.prompt: A dropdown shows only the legal next statuses. What is that?
choices: Complete enforcement of the rule on every path
A helpful reflection, not enforcement
A replacement for the model
A rule for the database
items.explanation: Other paths into the system never touch the dropdown.

items.prompt: A nightly job batch-cancels subscriptions. The grace-period rule exists only as the UI dropdown. What can happen?
choices: The job respects the dropdown automatically at run time
The job can skip the grace period undetected
The job fails because the UI is closed
The dropdown blocks the job at runtime
items.explanation: The UI is one door among several. A rule not in the model cannot constrain the others.
items.reference:
Stored field versus modeled rule
📦 status column: accepts any string
🚦 SubscriptionStatus: active, then grace period, then cancelled
💸 Discount: never above 40% without manager approval
Why: a field records what happened; a model enforces what the business allows to happen, whichever path the change comes through.
items.learnMore:
Capture the rule, not just the value

A domain model turns a rule an expert would say out loud into something the code refuses to violate. A bare field will accept any value, including ones the business forbids.

Common mistake

Putting the rule only in the screen, so a job or another service can bypass it.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you follow at work or home that is enforced only by habit. What would happen if someone new or an automated process skipped it?

The term's meaning, its neighbor and the translation

items.prompt: An organization grows from 5 teams to 10. How do the pairs to reconcile change?
choices: From 10 to 20, exactly twice as many
From 10 to 45, about 4.5 times as many
From 10 to 90, nine times as many

items.explanation: Teams doubled, pairs went from 10 to 45. Growth is faster than the team count.
items.reference:
Pairs outgrow teams
2 teams: 1 pair
4 teams: 6 pairs
10 teams: 45 pairs
n teams: n x (n - 1) / 2 pairs
Why: informal comparison works for a handful of teams; beyond that, the pairs outnumber what anyone can remember, so the record has to be written down.
items.learnMore:
A context map is a standing record

A context map lists which contexts exist, what each owns, and how a term translates at each boundary that matters. It replaces asking around, but only while it stays accurate.

Common mistake

Writing the map once and never updating it, so entries quietly mislead.
items.reflection: Think of a group that grew until word-of-mouth stopped working. What did they have to write down, and who kept it current?

items.prompt: A ten-team organization has a map, but two entries have drifted from what teams actually mean. Compared with having no map, how are they placed?
choices: Better, only if the stale entries get caught
Always worse, since a map should be perfect or absent
Always better, since any document helps
Unchanged, since nobody reads maps
items.explanation: A map gives people something concrete to check, but a trusted stale entry misleads silently. Its value depends on being kept current.

choices: No, it was to name two real concepts
Yes, Priya needed one winner to settle the report
Yes, the executive demanded it

choices: Marcus
Priya
The executive
Dana

items.prompt: What was Priya's role in the meeting?
choices: She chose Billing's definition
She wrote the database schema live in the meeting

She approved the executive's request

choices: One combined count of 6,000
1,200 Billing Accounts and 4,800 Support Contacts

items.prompt: What is an edge case?
choices: A rare case that tests whether a rule is clear
A case that never happens in practice
The most common case in the data
A case that only engineers care about
items.explanation: Vague definitions often break on unusual examples.

items.prompt: What does a fuzzy internal definition mean?
choices: Two teams define the word differently from each other
The word is spelled in two ways
The word is missing from the code
The team itself has no clear definition yet
items.explanation: Unlike a collision, the problem is inside one team.

items.prompt: Can a better name fix a concept nobody has pinned down?
choices: Yes, any well chosen name settles the question
Yes, if the name is short
No, the concept itself must be clarified
No, but only in large companies
items.explanation: A name labels a concept; it cannot create one.

items.prompt: What is the first step with a fuzzy definition?
choices: Rename it in the code
Ask domain experts about edge cases
Pick the most common meaning and move on
Wait for the next report
items.explanation: Edge-case questions force the substance into the open.

items.prompt: Someone opens a support ticket but has never paid anything. A Support Contact must belong to exactly one Billing Account. What does this edge case reveal?
choices: The ticket should be deleted
The definition has a gap that experts must settle
The rule about exactly one account is proven right
The contact belongs to the oldest account
items.explanation: A contact with no account contradicts the stated rule, so the definition is incomplete until experts decide what such a person is.
items.reference:
Two different problems
🤝 Collision: each team can state its definition, and they differ
🌫️ Fuzzy: a team cannot state its own definition consistently
🔍 Fix for fuzzy: ask experts about edge cases
Why: naming fixes a collision between clear concepts, but it cannot create a concept nobody has pinned down yet.
items.learnMore:
Edge cases make a vague definition precise

When a team's own meaning is unclear, a new name only hides that. Asking about unusual cases, such as a ticket from someone who never pays, forces the definition to become explicit.

Common mistake

Renaming a vague concept with a confident-sounding label and calling it solved.
